reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it promotes a DeFi liquidity pool as a way to obtain 10% per month conservatively and ties that return-focused claim to cryptocurrency participation. It also reports a 20% return over 60 days from a $592 liquidity pool, although the available video evidence does not establish a payment requirement, guaranteed outcome, actual transaction, or verified profit.

citations.quote: How to get 10% per month at #defi conservatively!
I showed a practical example where I made 20% in 60 days without even moving or checking the pool.
If you want to learn more subscribe to the channel!
it's just a liquidity pool that has been provided with $592
so far I've collected 121 dollars in this pool

opening.argument: Judge, read the return claim alongside the speaker's qualifications. He says building a liquidity pool while the market rises is difficult, suggests the outcome depends on the pair or range, and explicitly sets asset valuation aside when calculating his example. Those are material limits on what his percentage measures. The title is emphatic, but the spoken discussion is better understood as investment commentary about one pool than as a promise that viewers will earn the same return.

it depends, man, it must be with a bad par or range
I will ignore the asset valuation, ignore this here, ignore it
How to get 10% per month at #defi conservatively!

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening correctly identifies the title's return claim and the speaker's reported result, but neither establishes a guaranteed outcome or a request for the viewer to fund a pool. The speaker calls the calculation an example and excludes asset valuation from it. The invitation at the end is to subscribe to learn more, not to transfer funds. That narrower reading matters when deciding whether this is commentary or a solicitation.

citations.quote: I showed a practical example where I made 20% in 60 days
I will ignore the asset valuation, ignore this here, ignore it
If you want to learn more subscribe to the channel!

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Those qualifications do not undo the central pitch. The title tells viewers how to get a conservative 10% per month, while the description highlights a claimed 20% in 60 days without monitoring the pool. Excluding asset valuation makes the spoken calculation less complete; it does not turn the return-focused presentation into a risk warning. The speaker then connects the claimed percentage to money provided to a liquidity pool.

opening.argument: Judge, the speaker frames this as an answer to a disagreement about when liquidity pools are useful. He walks through a specific pool, identifies the amount provided, and explains how he calculated his reported percentage from the amount collected. That is a demonstration of a liquidity-pool example, not evidence that he is onboarding viewers into a particular scheme. Even the description calls it a practical example and invites viewers to subscribe to learn more.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution treats the title and the reported result as proof of a return-driven solicitation. But the description places the example in a discussion about whether liquidity pools are useful, and the speaker shows his arithmetic rather than claiming every viewer will obtain his result. The $592 is presented as the amount provided to the pool in his example, not an amount the audience is told to send.

citations.quote: the staff has questioned and doubted the usefulness of one of the best tools that are providing liquidity in the #Cryptocurrency market.
will give $121 divided by 592 20 percent
it's just a liquidity pool that has been provided with $592

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A worked example can still promote an investment return. Here the title offers a way to get 10% per month conservatively, and the description uses the speaker's claimed 20% in 60 days to support that message. Showing the calculation does not verify a net profit or establish that the highlighted result is representative. The educational framing does not erase the repeated emphasis on returns from liquidity provision.

citations.quote: How to get 10% per month at #defi conservatively!

I will ignore the asset valuation, ignore this here, ignore it

opening.argument: Judge, the observable call to action is ordinary channel promotion: viewers are asked to subscribe for more information. The speaker describes money already provided to a liquidity pool and an amount he says he collected; he does not, in the supplied speech, ask viewers to pay him, provide credentials, join a downline, or use a specified deposit route. A striking return headline warrants scrutiny, but the record supports promotion of the speaker's content more directly than it supports an identifiable transaction with viewers.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution itself notes that the available evidence does not establish a payment requirement, guaranteed outcome, actual transaction, or verified profit. Its cited subscription request points to the channel, while the $592 and $121 refer to the speaker's described pool example. The headline may overstate what that example proves, but it does not supply the missing viewer-facing payment or credential request.

citations.quote: If you want to learn more subscribe to the channel!
it's just a liquidity pool that has been provided with $592
so far I've collected 121 dollars in this pool

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The absence of a payment link or credential request does not make the return promotion ordinary channel commerce. The title offers a conservative 10% monthly DeFi return, and the description reinforces it with an asserted 20% result over 60 days. The speaker connects that result to funds provided to a liquidity pool. The evidence need not establish a viewer's completed transaction for the video to be promoting investment-pool returns.
